title: Unseen text pair: 'Our Library Must Stay' and 'Libraries in Numbers'
subject: English
source: Written for english/y7 lesson 59 (Unseen text pair 'Our Library Must Stay' (letter) and 'Libraries in Numbers' (information article), both teacher-written (pupil PDF))
intro: Lesson 59. Two teacher-written texts. Read both, then compare how the writers present the library.

passage.title: Text A: Our Library Must Stay (a letter)
paras: I am writing because our library on Station Road is in danger of closing, and I believe that closing it would close a door on hundreds of people.

When my family first came to this town, I could not read English well. Every Saturday the librarian, Mrs Clarke, found me a book that was just hard enough. Ten years later, I am studying to become a teacher. Where else could a child sit, warm and safe, among thousands of stories, for free?

Some say people read on their phones now. Perhaps. But a phone cannot help a grandmother fill in a form, or give a quiet table to a student whose home is crowded. A library is not a building full of books. It is a door. Please, do not close it.

passage.title: Text B: Libraries in Numbers (an information article)
paras: Libraries across the country are changing. In the town of Brookfield, visits to the central library fell by a fifth in ten years, from about 150,000 a year to about 120,000. Over the same period, online loans of e-books and audiobooks doubled.

Libraries now offer more than books. Many run computer help sessions, homework clubs and activities for toddlers. In Brookfield, the number of people using the library's free computers has stayed steady, and most are adults looking for work or completing official forms.

Councils face difficult choices. Running a library costs money for staff, heating and new stock, and some councils have reduced opening hours or moved libraries into shared buildings. Others have kept them open with the help of volunteers.
(Brookfield is a made-up town; the figures are examples for this exercise.)

questions.q: Retrieve one fact from Text B.
questions.a: Visits fell by a fifth in ten years, or online loans doubled.

questions.q: Retrieve one opinion from Text A.
questions.a: Closing it would close a door on hundreds of people (or a library is a door).
Text A: to persuade; Text B: to inform.

questions.q: Compare how the writers present the library.
questions.a: Text A presents it as a lifeline using anecdote and the metaphor 'a door'; Text B presents a changing service with statistics and a formal tone.

questions.q: Retrieve one fact from Text B and one opinion from Text A
questions.a: Fact: visits fell by a fifth in ten years (or online loans doubled). Opinion: closing it would close a door on hundreds of people.
Text A: to persuade; Text B: to inform.

questions.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a comparative PEEDL paragraph: 'Compare how the writers present the library.' Starter: 'Both writers..., however...'
questions.a: A PEEDL paragraph comparing purpose, viewpoint and method with evidence from both texts.

questions.q: Extend: complete the comparison grid with one more method from each text
questions.a: For example: Text A rhetorical question; Text B formal, third person.

questions.q: Stretch: which text would persuade a council more? Explain
questions.a: A judgement weighing emotion against evidence.

questions.q: Which is the best comparative sentence?
options: Text A uses a personal story to persuade, whereas Text B uses statistics to inform.
Text A is a letter. Text B is an article.
questions.a: B) Text A uses a personal story to persuade, whereas Text B uses statistics to inform.. It compares method and purpose in one sentence with a connective.

questions.q: Text B was written mainly to...
Answer the ponder: can two people describe the same place and both be right?
questions.a: For example: yes; each is honest from a different viewpoint and purpose.
